section.title: Managing managers changes the consequences of small actions
section.deck: A Meta senior manager explains why wider organizational scope requires new interaction habits.

blocks.question: What skill gaps appear when a first-line manager steps into a manager-of-managers role?
answer: The guest emphasizes learning how to add value to the managers who report to you. A more senior role changes which interventions help and which undermine the organization. He illustrates this with a skip-level meeting in which a newly promoted leader asks leading questions about an employee’s manager. The employee may start relying on the senior leader instead, while the manager feels bypassed and weakened.

The important failure is not simply having the meeting. It is overlooking how questions and judgments propagate through a management chain. Small actions become magnified across multiple relationships. The guest says these subtleties are often learned through observation and practice, not only from reading about management.

He expects some mistakes during the transition, just as new managers make mistakes when moving from individual contribution. A promotion decision should therefore consider the support around the person: whether their own leader can help them recognize and repair problems. Strategy and organizational design also matter, but early interaction errors can cause damage before those longer-term responsibilities become the main issue.
blocks.speaker: Meta senior manager

blocks.question: How do individual-contributor and management growth compare, and are they meritocratic?
answer: He says that evaluation becomes more opaque at high levels in either path. In calibration discussions, a person may be associated with a valuable initiative without having been instrumental in its success. The same attribution problem applies to managers. A short review period can make it difficult to separate a persuasive account from a clearly demonstrated contribution.

Longer observation can clarify the picture: a leader who repeatedly produces good outcomes over several years is easier to assess than someone in one half-year cycle. He thinks some senior IC and first-line-management work is more visible to an outside observer, while higher-level work often requires access to the internal details and leadership chain.

He does not offer a simple verdict that one ladder is fair and the other unfair. His concern is insufficient evidence and accountability when the relevant impact is hard to trace. The resulting frustration is real for employees with limited visibility, and a desire for fairness does not automatically create the data needed to judge it.
